issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s bona fide release claim is to be considered liberally when the landlord offers the tenant reasonably suitable accommodation, and comparative hardship may establish that the statutory requirement for release is met.
material_facts: The landlord sought release of the tenant’s accommodation for his own bona fide use.
The authorities found that refusing release would cause greater hardship to the landlord, who was living in rented premises and would be deprived of the beneficial enjoyment of his own property.
The landlord offered his rented accommodation to the tenant in exchange, but the tenant did not accept the proposal.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s claim was entitled to liberal consideration. On the findings of greater hardship to the landlord, refusal of the application would deprive him of the beneficial enjoyment of his own property, and the fourth proviso’s requirement was satisfied.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, read with its fourth proviso and Rule 16(1)(f) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972, requires consideration of comparative hardship. Under Rule 16(1)(f), where a landlord seeking accommodation for bona fide personal or family use offers the tenant reasonably suitable accommodation, the landlord’s claim is to be considered liberally. The Court applied the analogous balancing approach discussed in Bhaichand Ratanshi v. Laxmishanker Tribhovan, including that alternative accommodation is important but not decisive and that hardship depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. That judgment also referred to Sims v. Wilson, Fowle v. Bell, Smith v. Penny, Chandler v. Strevett and Kelley v. Goodwin.

predicates.landlord_release_proceeding: A landlord sought release of accommodation occupied by a tenant for the landlord’s own use or the use of family members.
predicates.bona_fide_personal_need: The landlord’s need for the accommodation for personal or family use was found to be genuine.
predicates.reasonably_suitable_alternative_offered: The landlord offered the tenant other accommodation reasonably suitable for the tenant’s needs.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks release for a genuine personal or family need and offers the tenant reasonably suitable alternative accommodation, the landlord’s claim is considered liberally.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court errs by setting aside concurrent findings supporting release when those findings disclose no infirmity.
material_facts: The Prescribed Authority found the landlord’s need bona fide and found that refusal would cause the landlord greater hardship.
The revisional court reached the same conclusions after considering the comparative hardship to the landlord and tenant.
The High Court set aside the release orders, but the Supreme Court found no infirmity in the lower authorities’ orders or findings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was in error in interfering with the release orders; its judgment was set aside and the orders granting release were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Applying Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, and its fourth proviso, the Court held that the concurrent findings on bona fide need and comparative hardship disclosed no infirmity warranting the High Court’s interference.

rule.if: appeal_from_high_court_order and landlord_release_proceeding and concurrent_findings_support_release and no_infirmity_in_lower_orders

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_order: A party appealed from a High Court order that had set aside an order granting release of rented accommodation.
predicates.landlord_release_proceeding: A landlord sought release of accommodation occupied by a tenant for the landlord’s own use or the use of family members.
predicates.concurrent_findings_support_release: The lower authorities both found the landlord’s need bona fide and concluded that refusal of release would cause the landlord greater hardship.
predicates.no_infirmity_in_lower_orders: The Supreme Court found no defect in the lower authorities’ orders or findings.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a High Court order setting aside release, the lower authorities made concurrent findings supporting release, and their orders disclose no infirmity, the High Court’s interference is unwarranted.
